\chapter{Where You Are From}
\label{ch:ml-origin}
\hlchaptermodality{80}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer where I am from with a place rather than with a category, and say that somebody is a Malayali.}

From cold: the three place words in order of scale, the person word and where it came from, and the fact that placing somebody needs no new grammar at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ūrŭ]{\ml{ഊര്} (ūrŭ) — town}

\label{lesson:ML-C80-uuru}



\begin{quote}
What was \emph{nāṭŭ}? And when somebody asks you which one you are from, what could you say back?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഊര്}}
\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} — \emph{ūrŭ} — a town, a village, the settled place somebody is from.

\emph{nāṭŭ} was handed to you with a warning printed inside it: \textbf{its scale floats.} A \emph{nāṭŭ} can be a country, a district or a home region, and the situation decides which. That is useful and it is also why the question \emph{which nāṭŭ are you from} was, until now, a question you could not answer — you had the word for the category and no word for a place.

\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} pins the small end down. Where \emph{nāṭŭ} floats, \emph{ūrŭ} is \textbf{the settlement} — somewhere with houses in it and a name.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{covers} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} \emph{ūrŭ} & one settled place \\
\textbf{\ml{നാട്}} \emph{nāṭŭ} & anything from a district to a country \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It is an old word and a shared one. Tamil says \emph{ūr} for the same thing, and it is buried in place-names the length of the south — so a name you cannot read yet may still end in a piece you now know.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The small end of the question you have been able to hear since the ground words, and not answer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ūrŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nāṭŭ}, then \emph{ūrŭ}, and say which of the two has a fixed size
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is an \emph{ūrŭ}? (\textbf{A town — one settled place}.) And which is the wider word, \emph{ūrŭ} or \emph{nāṭŭ}? (\emph{\textbf{nāṭŭ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kēraḷaṁ indya]{\ml{കേരളം} \ml{ഇന്ത്യ} (kēraḷaṁ, indya) — Kerala and India}

\label{lesson:ML-C80-keralam}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for a town, and say the wider word it sits inside.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കേരളം}, \ml{ഇന്ത്യ}}
\textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} — \emph{kēraḷaṁ} — Kerala, the state this language is spoken in.

\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} — \emph{indya} — India, the country Kerala is part of.

Until this page, every place word you owned named a \textbf{kind} of place: ground, forest, home country, town. None of them named \textbf{one}. These two do, and that is the whole difference between describing where you are from and saying it.

Now the floating word has fixed points to float between:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} \emph{ūrŭ} & a town \\
\textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} \emph{kēraḷaṁ} & Kerala \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} \emph{indya} & India \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Each of the three can answer \emph{which nāṭŭ are you from}, and choosing among them is the same choice English makes when it answers that question with a town, a region or a country: \textbf{you pick the one your listener will recognise.}

Say \emph{kēraḷaṁ} slowly and you will hear the retroflex \textbf{\ml{ള}} in the middle of it — the sound you met in the name of the language itself. It is the same letter doing the same work, and it is worth noticing that the place and the tongue spoken there are built on the same sound.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An answer, where you had only a category.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kēraḷaṁ}
  \item \emph{indya}
  \item the three place words in order, smallest first
  \item which of the three you would give to somebody far away
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two is the state? (\emph{\textbf{kēraḷaṁ}}.) Which is the country? (\emph{\textbf{indya}}.) And which sound sits in the middle of the first one? (\textbf{The retroflex \ml{ള}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[malayāḷi]{\ml{മലയാളി} (malayāḷi) — a Malayali}

\label{lesson:ML-C80-malayali}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I speak Malayalam}, the sentence you have owned since almost the beginning. Then say the name of the state.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മലയാളി}}
\textbf{\ml{മലയാളി}} — \emph{malayāḷi} — a Malayali: a person of Kerala, a speaker of this language.

You have had most of this word since your fifth chapter's sentence. Put the two side by side and only the tail is different:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{മലയാള}}\ml{ം} \emph{malayāḷaṁ} & the language \\
\textbf{\ml{മലയാള}}\ml{ി} \emph{malayāḷi} & the person \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Everything up to the last piece is shared. \textbf{-\ml{ം} ends the language, -\ml{ി} ends the person}, and you can see the join without being told where it is.

\begin{culture}
The language word is itself built out of two older pieces — \textbf{\ml{മല}} \emph{mala}, a hill, and a second piece meaning a place. \textbf{The language is named after the country it grew in}, and the person is then named after the language rather than after the state.

So the chain runs \textbf{hill $\to$ land $\to$ language $\to$ person}, and \emph{malayāḷi} sits at the far end of it. Nobody has to tell you that Kerala is hilly for the word to make sense; the word has been saying so the whole time.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Malayalam has no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}Keralite\textquotedblright{}}]
English keeps two shapes for this job — \emph{India} the place and \textbf{Indian} the describing word, \emph{Kerala} and \emph{Keralite}. Malayalam keeps \textbf{one}.

\textbf{\ml{മലയാളി} is a person-word, not a describing word}, and when you need it to describe somebody you do what this language always does: \textbf{stand it in front, unchanged.}

\textbf{\ml{മലയാളി} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ}} — \emph{malayāḷi adhyāpakan} — a Malayali teacher.

That is the rule you already have. A quality word stands in front of the thing; a degree word stands in front of the quality; and a person-word used to place somebody stands in front too, with nothing added and nothing altered. \textbf{The gentilic costs you no new grammar at all} — which is the reason it waited until now rather than arriving with the place names.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to say where somebody is from, and the discovery that it needed no machinery.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{malayāḷaṁ}, then \emph{malayāḷi}, and say where they part
  \item \emph{malayāḷi adhyāpakan}
  \item what you had to add to \emph{malayāḷi} to make it describe the teacher
  \item the two older pieces the language word is built from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{malayāḷi}? (\textbf{A person of Kerala, a speaker of this language}.) Which ending makes the person out of the language? (\textbf{-\ml{ി}}.) And what changes when you put the word in front of another one? (\textbf{Nothing.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[evideyāṇŭ enna ōrmma]{(where you are from) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R80-origin-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say the floating word for a home region, and then say the word that pins its small end down.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a scale, and a person on it}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} \emph{ūrŭ} & a town \\
\textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} \emph{kēraḷaṁ} & Kerala \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} \emph{indya} & India \\
\textbf{\ml{മലയാളി}} \emph{malayāḷi} & a person from there \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The first three answer \emph{which nāṭŭ are you from}, and you pick among them the way English does: \textbf{the one your listener will recognise.} The fourth is not a place at all — it is the person, built out of the language word you have owned since almost the beginning, with the tail changed:

\textbf{\ml{മലയാള}}\ml{ം} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{മലയാള}}\ml{ി}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The answer to a question you have been able to \emph{hear} for a long time.

And the chapter's real finding is what it did \textbf{not} need. English carries two shapes — \emph{India} and \textbf{Indian}, \emph{Kerala} and \emph{Keralite}. Malayalam carries one, and places somebody by \textbf{standing the person-word in front, unchanged}:

\textbf{\ml{മലയാളി} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ}} — \emph{malayāḷi adhyāpakan} — a Malayali teacher.

That is the same rule as the quality word before the thing and the degree word before the quality. \textbf{Three different jobs, one position, nothing altered.} When a language reuses a position this hard, learning the position is worth more than learning any of the words that fill it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three place words, smallest first
  \item \emph{malayāḷi}
  \item where \emph{malayāḷi} came from, and which piece of it is new
  \item \emph{malayāḷi adhyāpakan}
  \item what had to change about \emph{malayāḷi} to put it in front of the teacher
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word names one settled place? (\emph{\textbf{ūrŭ}}.) Which word names the person rather than the place? (\emph{\textbf{malayāḷi}}.) And how many shapes does Malayalam keep for that job, where English keeps two? (\textbf{One.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ūṇ · vēṇō · allē · malayāḷi]{\ml{ഊണ്} · \ml{വേണോ} · \ml{അല്ലേ} — asking, offering, and checking}

\label{lesson:ML-R80-what-came-once}



\begin{quote}
The word for a meal. Say it, then offer one — the asking form of \emph{want}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: three moves that need each other}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item offer a meal — \emph{ūṇ vēṇō?}
  \item check that you have understood — \emph{allē?}
  \item the meal word again, and say which verb it is built from
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\ml{വേണോ}} is not a separate word for \emph{do you want}: it is the wanting word wearing the question ending the book taught long before. \textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} does the opposite job — it does not ask a question so much as invite the other person to agree with one you have already answered.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ml{മലയാളി}} is the language word with a person ending on it, and that is worth holding because English does not build words this way reliably. The pattern is productive: a place or a tongue plus the ending gives you the people of it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ml{ഗ}} — name the letter, cold
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} ask for information, or for agreement? (\textbf{Agreement.}) What does the ending on \textbf{\ml{മലയാളി}} do to the language word? (\textbf{Makes a person of it.})
\end{tcolorbox}
